files.text:
Rain on paper

A raindrop is three or four millimetres across, about a twentieth of a teaspoon of water. Let one fall on a sheet of good writing paper and for a moment it stands up as a bead, held off by the size the papermaker put into the sheet; then it sinks, and the water runs out between the fibres as a widening grey disc, quickly at first and then more and more slowly, a little further along the grain than across it. Wet paper is darker and half transparent, because the water has filled the air between the fibres that used to scatter the light back, and the writing on the other side comes through. Iron-gall ink, the old black, would barely move: its iron is bound into the paper. But the blue sold for fountain pens for most of the last century is a dye, made to wash out of a shirt cuff, and the rain takes it up again and carries it along.

Roundstone, 14th August

Dear Una,

I am writing this at the table under the fuchsia, between showers, because your father has the kitchen full of onions drying on the Connacht Tribune. It has rained on all but four days since you left. It comes in off the Atlantic in grey sheets over Inishnee, and you can stand at the gate and watch one cross the bay like somebody walking, and count to forty before it reaches the hedge.

The garden doesn't mind. The gunnera by the stream is up past the shed roof, the montbretia is through the wall again, and the Kerr's Pinks in the lazy beds are the best in years, floury, they break in the pot. The slugs are the size of your thumb. I go out at night with the torch and a jar of salt water and I am not one bit sorry.

Tell me what the heat is like. Tell me the colour of the ground. I can't picture a place where you have to water a garden.

Your loving mother,

Maura

P.S. There's another one coming in over the island now, I can see it on the water. I'll bring this in.

P.P.S. Mrs Joyce asks were you anywhere near the fires. I told her it is a very big country. Your father says to tell you the hay is in, all of it, dry, which he calls a miracle and I call the four days.

Washable blue is not one dye but two or three, and they let go of the paper at different rates. As the wet spreads, the most loosely held runs on ahead and the edge of the stain goes turquoise, while the line it came from is left a shade more violet: the separation a chemistry class makes with a strip of filter paper standing in a jar of water. When the shower passes, the water leaves from the thin edges first, and more flows outward from the middle to replace it, bringing whatever it has dissolved: dye, dust, the paper's own size. All of it is set down at the last line to dry, the tide line, the same ring a cup leaves on a table. Conservators read the history of a damp archive in them, one ring inside another, each a shower or a leaking roof, and the ink feathered sideways along the fibres, still blue.

# pretext-rain A handwritten letter left out on a garden table, and a shower coming over it as you scroll. The first drops sit on the sheet as glossy beads and sink into dark round spots; the fountain-pen ink in their way redissolves and bleeds out with the water, the line left a shade more violet and the edge of the stain turquoise. The shower thickens, the spots join, the sheet goes dark and half-transparent so the postscript on the back shows through, mirrored; where the drips off the hedge fall hardest the water stands and runs down the sheet and takes the ink with it. Then it stops, and the wet dries from the edges in, leaving tide lines and the writing soft and feathered where it ran. Scroll back and the letter is dry and fresh again. ```html

Roundstone, 14th August

Dear Una,

I am writing this at the table under the fuchsia …

The garden doesn't mind …

Your loving mother,

Maura

P.S. There's another one coming in over the island now …

P.P.S. Mrs Joyce asks …

``` Or `import { pretextRain } from './pretext-rain.js'` and call `pretextRain(section, options)`; it returns `destroy()`. The paragraphs are read in order. Classes set their place on the sheet: `pr-date` (right-aligned), `pr-greet`, plain `

` (body, first line indented), `pr-close` (from 40% in), `pr-sign` (from 58%), `pr-ps`. A `pr-verso` paragraph is written on the back of the sheet: it is only seen through the paper, mirrored, faintly when dry and clearly where wet. 150-220 words on the front fit well. The face is the `.pr-letter`'s own `font-family` (the demo loads Homemade Apple, which reads as a real pen and stays legible at 11px on a phone). ## Options Data attributes on the section, or the options object (which wins). | attribute | option | default | what it does | |---|---|---|---| | `data-seed` | `seed` | `7` | The sheet's fibres and flocs, the cockle, the drop schedule and where the downpour falls hardest. `random` gives a new shower each visit (the default is tuned so the run crosses the writing). | | `data-heavy` | `heavy` | `1` | How hard the shower comes down: scales the downpour (drops and the standing water that makes rivulets). `0.5` is a passing shower; `2` washes most of the letter out. | | `data-aspect` | `aspect` | `1.38` | Sheet height / width (a phone may make it taller, up to 1.7). | | `data-leading` | `leading` | `1.85` | Line pitch, x the font size. | | `data-font`, `data-weight` | `font`, `weight` | the letter's | Canvas-only face, if it should differ from the fallback's. | ## The real thing What a real observer sees, and what is modelled: - **A drop on writing paper.** A raindrop is 2-4 mm across. On sized paper it stands as a bead for a moment, then sinks; 80 gsm paper holds about 6 µL/cm², so one drop wets a spot 1.5-2.5 cm across. *Modelled:* each drop lands as a dome of standing water (a bead, which refracts the writing under it and catches the sky); the paper takes it up only as fast as it has room and the water wicks outward, so the bead drains as the spot grows. - **Wicking.** The wet disc grows roughly as the square root of time (Lucas-Washburn) and stops when the water is spread thin; it reaches a little further along the grain, and its front is ragged at the scale of fibre flocs. *Modelled:* nonlinear diffusion (mobility ∝ water²), so fronts are sharp and slow as they thin; faster along the grain (+30%) and along individual fibres (short segments, mostly with the grain, that wick up to twice as fast along their length: this is what feathers the ink); slower in the dense flocs of the real sheet (its formation, from the scan). - **Wet paper.** Darker and more transparent: water fills the air gaps that scatter light. *Modelled:* wet paper is darkened and greyed, the sheet's cloudy formation comes up, and the writing on the back shows through, mirrored (also, very faintly, when dry). - **Washable blue ink is a dye, and more than one.** Water redissolves it and the moving water carries it; each dye shares itself between the water and the cellulose in its own ratio, so the run separates as in paper chromatography. *Modelled:* two dyes, violet (held hard) and turquoise (runs), which together make royal blue by Beer-Lambert absorption. The line keeps its violet, the stain's edge goes turquoise. Iron-gall ink would hardly move; this letter is written in washable blue. - **A downpour.** Once the paper is saturated, water stands on it, gathers in the valleys of the cockle and runs down the sloping sheet in narrow rivulets that carry dissolved dye. *Modelled:* a downpour adds an even film where it falls hardest (drips from the hedge above the table). A single bead on sized paper stays put (a high pinning depth), so a word that got wet stays where it is; under the downpour, and along the rivulets traced from the bottom of that patch down the valleys of the cockle, the pinning is low and standing water flows to the three cells below, split by the slope of the sheet, carrying its dye. The ink runs only there. - **Drying and tide lines.** Evaporation is fastest at the thin edge of a wet patch, so water flows outward from the middle and leaves its dissolved matter at the last line to dry (Deegan et al. 1997, the coffee ring). The wet area shrinks from the edges in. *Modelled:* evaporation three times faster at the edge; the paper's own solubles (size, lignin, dirt) dissolve and ride the water, so the ground the water covered is left cleaner. The tide line is drawn once, where that cleaned ground ends: sharp and darkest on its outer edge, fading inward over a few px, brown-yellow. - **Cockle.** Wet fibres swell and the sheet buckles into soft waves along the grain, and keeps some of it when dry. *Modelled* as shading only. Simplified: one layer of paper (no through-thickness flow, so the back's writing does not run), no splash crowns (a splash is a few satellite droplets), no wind, and the sheet does not move. The verso's ink is drawn, not simulated. ## How it works 1. **Writing.** pretext (Cheng Lou) prepares each paragraph once at 100px; a binary search re-sets the letter at eighteen trial sizes and keeps the largest that fills the sheet, with ragged `layoutNextLine` lines. Each line is written onto a canvas at device resolution with a hand's irregularities (a drifting baseline, a slight slope, ink running drier between dips of the pen). The back is written the same way, mirrored. 2. **The paper.** A grid of 200 cells across the sheet (the same on every screen, so the shower is the same everywhere). Fixed fields: permeability and fibres; the cockle and the downhill split for standing water; the written ink per cell (each dye's starting place). 3. **One step** is three passes of one fragment shader with two outputs (RGBA32F water: in paper, standing, solubles dissolved and fixed; RGBA16F dye: violet and turquoise, fixed and dissolved). Fluxes are computed the same way from both sides of every link, so water and dye are conserved. 4. **The shower** is a seeded schedule over 2400 steps: a few first drops, thickening, a downpour, easing off, then drying. Scroll progress picks the step; the simulation steps forward to it (up to ~40 steps a frame, adapting to the frame time). Every 200 steps the state is copied to a checkpoint, so scrolling back restores the nearest checkpoint and steps forward from there: exact and quick. While it replays, the last good frame stays up. 5. **Drawing.** The state is smoothed with a cubic B-spline when sampled. The written line comes from the crisp ink texture, scaled by how much of each dye is left in its cell. Where it has been wet, it spreads out from the stroke in every direction: a soft violet halo hugging it and a wider turquoise one, both broken into fine tendrils by a fibre texture stretched along the grain (no offset copies). The dye that has really moved (the drip patch, the rivulet, the edges of big drops) is drawn from the grid. Paper is the real sheet. Beads and films of water refract, darken at the rim, and carry a soft sky and a small highlight. A **tap** lets one drop fall where you tap: it is inserted into the timeline at the current step and given 160 steps to soak in (about three seconds). Scrolling back past that step removes it; scrolling forward again brings it back. **Enter** on the focused stage drops one somewhere on the letter. ## Events | event | detail | when | |---|---|---| | `pretext-rain:drop` | `{ x, y, size, tap, intensity }` (stage px, size as a fraction of the sheet width, intensity in drops per step) | a drop lands, scrolling forward (at most three per frame), or a tap | ## Tuning All in `build()` (`SIM` uniforms) and the schedule functions: - `uDw` wicking speed (stable up to ~0.085 with three passes a step); `uKa` how fast standing water soaks in; `uScrit` the pinning depth for a bead (3.5 under the downpour and along the rivulets), `uSr` how fast standing water runs. - `uKb` how hard each dye (violet, turquoise) and the solubles hold to the fibres: raise the first two to keep the letter more legible. `uDis`/`uAds` how fast they dissolve and set again. `uDm` diffusion within the water. - `rate(f)` drops per step over the shower, `film(f)` the downpour, `evap(f)` drying, the drip mask in `staticFields()`. - Look: the wet tint (about 10% darker, the cream deepening to oatmeal, the sheet's texture stronger), show-through, dye absorbances `kA`/`kB`, the halos (`haloA`, `haloB`), tide-line strength and cockle `amp` in `SHEET_FS`. ## Theming | variable | default | used for | |---|---|---| | `--pr-sheet` | `#f6f0e2` | the sheet's tint (multiplied with the real paper) | | `--pr-ink` | `#1f3277` | the plain letter's ink (fallback) | | `--pr-hand` | Homemade Apple | the face (the canvas copies the `.pr-letter`'s font) | | `--pr-runway` | `280svh` | length of the scroll runway | | `--gutter` | | side padding of the plain letter | The stage greys a few per cent while the shower is overhead. ## Accessibility and motion - The letter is real text in the DOM: read aloud, found by ctrl+F, printed. Once the canvas is live it is visually hidden; the canvas is `aria-hidden`. - Without JS, WebGL2 or float render targets it is the plain letter on the real paper. - Reduced motion: no runway, the letter after the shower, dried, with tide lines and feathered ink, still readable in most places. A tap still lets a drop fall (shown soaked in at once). - The stage is focusable (Enter drops a drop) and `touch-action: pan-y`: a vertical swipe always scrolls. ## Cost - Simulation: ~55k cells, three passes a step, ~30 texture reads a cell a pass. It runs only while the scroll position (or a tapped drop) is ahead of the state, at most ~40 steps a frame, fewer if frames run long; a full fling through the whole shower catches up in about a second. Checkpoints are made lazily: at most 13, ~1.3 MB each. - Drawing: one fragment pass over the sheet, ~90 texture reads a pixel (cubic samples), only when the state changed. Canvas DPR capped at 2. - Idle, off screen or in a hidden tab: nothing runs. ## Credits - [pretext](https://github.com/chenglou/pretext) by Cheng Lou, MIT (`vendor/pretext`, unmodified, see its `LICENSE` and `VERSION`). - The paper: a blank leaf from a sketchbook of Alexander Cozens, Yale Center for British Art, CC0 (`assets/credits.json`). - Homemade Apple by Font Diner, via Google Fonts (Apache 2.0), loaded by the demo. - The letter and the paragraphs around it were written for this component.
